about.title: Cupertino Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Cupertino's mix of tech-corridor traffic and residential streets creates a steady flow of vehicles along De Anza Boulevard, Stevens Creek Boulevard, SR-85, and I-280. Public records show 160 injury collisions and 208 injured people in the most recent final year, with reported crashes clustering on Tuesday afternoons between 3 and 5 p.m. — likely tied to commute and school pickup patterns near the tech campuses and local schools. If you were hurt in one of these collisions, the period right after matters: photos fade from memory, vehicles get repaired or scrapped, and insurance adjusters move quickly to lock in a version of events. We handle personal injury claims directly, evaluating what happened, managing communication with insurers, and explaining your options under California law before you sign anything.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Before the Insurer

items.title: California's Two-Year Clock Is Shorter Than You Think
items.desc: You generally have two years from the crash date to file a car accident lawsuit in California, but that window shrinks dramatically — sometimes to six months — if a government vehicle or roadway defect was involved. We can flag that early so you don't lose the claim before you even realize the deadline applies.

items.title: Comparative Fault Means Partial Blame Doesn't End Your Case
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for a Stevens Creek or SR-85 collision, you can still recover a reduced share of damages. Insurers sometimes use shared-fault arguments to minimize payouts, which is where our legal guidance matters.

items.title: No Cap on Non-Economic Damages, No Upfront Cost to You
items.desc: California doesn't limit pain-and-suffering damages in standard car accident cases, and we work on contingency — meaning there's no fee unless you recover. That structure lets you get advice on your De Anza Boulevard or I-280 crash without adding financial pressure.

items.question: Should I give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company?
items.answer: It's generally wise to avoid giving a recorded statement before speaking with an attorney. Insurers often use recorded statements to find inconsistencies or minimize your claim later. We can advise you on what, if anything, to say.

items.question: What if my crash happened at a Cupertino intersection with no clear fault?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still pursue compensation even if fault is disputed or shared. We can review police reports, witness accounts, and traffic patterns — like those seen on De Anza or Stevens Creek — to help clarify what happened.

items.question: How long do I have to take legal action after a car accident in Cupertino?
items.answer: California generally allows two years from the date of the accident to file a lawsuit, though claims involving a government entity, like a city-maintained road, can have deadlines as short as six months. Because these timelines vary by circumstance, it's best to get an evaluation sooner rather than later.
